lore_anchors.definition: Ritual tablets held by officials during imperial ceremonies; made of bone, ivory, or wood, they symbolize rank and reverence in Confucian court ritual.
The highest form of kowtow in Chinese imperial ritual, reserved for Heaven, Earth, the emperor, and the ancestral temple; each kneeling cycle includes three head-to-ground bows.

In Chinese geomancy and political cosmology, the underground energy channel that determines a dynasty's legitimacy; the novel literalizes it as a parasitic power that must be borne through self-sacrifice.
A stolen fragment of divine power that holds up reality in the Dao-Twisted World; it can only be supported by a family willing to commit self-slaughter, making it a curse as much as a blessing.
An imperial artifact combining jade exterior and paper interior used for reading sacred edicts; in the Dao-Twisted World, the pages move like living animals.
The sarcophagus containing the previous emperors of Great Liang; its occupants are twisted by the Dragon Vein’s burden into monstrous forms.
The highest-ranking court Daoist or esoteric advisor, responsible for overseeing state rituals involving the Mandate of Heaven and Dragon Vein.
Physical markers of the emperor’s transformation into a “true dragon” (真龙天子), a folkloric symbol of legitimate rule; here literalized through body horror.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Gao Zhijian’s skin split during the enthronement?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The Mandate of Heaven is a violent, parasitic force that physically merges with the new emperor; the skin splitting is the literal cost of bearing the Dragon Vein’s power.
In the Dao-Twisted World, the Dragon Vein is the stolen fragment of divine power that holds up reality; it must be carried by the imperial family through constant self-sacrifice.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why is Li Huowang upset even though the ceremony succeeded?
cultural_notes_faq.a: He’s worried about Gao Zhijian’s fate—the previous emperor Ji Lin was twisted into a walking corpse. He’s also still bitter about Zhuge Yuan lying to him.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What are the “three kneels and nine prostrations”?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The highest form of reverence in Chinese imperial ritual; the subject kneels three times and touches the ground nine times, used for Heaven, Earth, the emperor, and the ancestors.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why do the eunuchs chant in such a strange, high voice?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The high-pitched, chanting style (宣诏/宣制) is a traditional court vocal technique used to project authority and ceremony; eunuchs’ voices naturally retain a higher timbre after castration.
